focus: Ruder (2016), An overview of gradient descent optimization algorithms, Sections 2.1 and 4.1. Explain gradient descent on the one-dimensional quadratic J(theta) = a/2 (theta - theta*)^2. Show the sequence of iterates on the loss curve, the loss after each step, and the step sizes. Let the learner change the learning rate and the starting point and switch momentum on/off. Guide them through a learning rate that converges smoothly and one that oscillates or diverges. Check that a learning rate of 1/a reaches the minimum in one step without momentum and that the iterates diverge when the learning rate exceeds 2/a without momentum; handle a starting point already at the minimum.
excerpt: (paraphrased) 2.1 Batch gradient descent updates the parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient of the objective: theta = theta - eta * grad J(theta). The learning rate eta determines the size of the steps taken to reach a minimum. A learning rate that is too small leads to slow convergence, while one that is too large can hinder convergence and cause the loss to fluctuate around the minimum or even diverge. 4.1 Momentum helps accelerate gradient descent in the relevant direction and dampens oscillations by adding a fraction gamma of the previous update vector to the current one: v_t = gamma v_{t-1} + eta grad J(theta), theta = theta - v_t. The momentum term gamma is usually set to 0.9 or a similar value.
